courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
md: Tiered storage moves *old* data to S3 and leaves the write path alone. S3-native moves the *write path itself* to S3, trading commit latency for stateless compute. Hybrids like Neon put a small quorum log in front so commits stay fast while object storage holds the bulk.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: Alert on symptoms, not causes. The SRE book's advice is to focus much more effort on catching symptoms than causes, and to worry about a cause only when it is very definite and very imminent. A page saying "cache hit rate dropped" is a cause; a page saying "users are burning the checkout budget at 20x" is a symptom, and it stays correct when the cause next time is something else.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Layout-aware models add *where* to *what*: each word's box becomes embedding lookups, so a model can learn that a value sits right of its key. OCR-free models fold reading into the network and emit structure directly.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Linux capabilities: splitting root into pieces
md: `docker run --privileged` gives the container all capabilities and access to all host devices (Docker documentation). Treat it as running the workload as root on the host. The same goes for adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_SYS_MODULE` "just for one feature".

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Red lines in this course: no locating, profiling or tracking of specific private individuals; no misrepresentation to get access; no use of credentials or data from breaches; no publishing of personal details. Worked examples use your own organisation, a fictional company (Northwind, under the reserved `.example` domain) or public institutions and already-public cases.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Metadata: what photos and documents say about themselves
md: Files describe themselves. Read metadata as one clue that needs corroboration; remove it from everything you publish.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Check only your own accounts, or colleagues' with their consent. Looking up someone else's email in breach data or a broker profile, without a lawful basis, is exactly the profiling this course rules out.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Prefix caching never changes outputs. It reuses KV for exactly the same tokens instead of recomputing it, so its effects are on speed and memory (outputs can differ only by the tiny floating-point noise any change in batching causes). It helps exactly as much as prefill dominates the work and prefixes repeat.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Verifying findings safely, without becoming the incident
md: Verify with the least risky evidence that answers the question. Write down the confidence and what you chose not to do. Stop immediately when you see signs that someone else got there first.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
md: Missing callers, a detached tower over [unknown], or hex instead of names are not hot spots. They are profiler blind spots. Fix frame pointers or symbols before you trust the picture.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
md: The one thing to remember: phishing attacks a decision, not a machine. Defences therefore come in three kinds: stop the message arriving, make the action harmless if taken (for example passkeys, logins that only work on the real site; lesson 12), and make the final step need a second check (for example calling the supplier on a known number).

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Lookalike domains and homoglyphs
md: Misconception: "hover over the link and check the domain" solves this. A homoglyph domain can look correct even when you hover, and on phones you often cannot hover. Machine checks (skeletons, domain age) and phishing-resistant logins (lesson 12) carry the load; human checks are a backup.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Byte order: reading and writing multi-byte fields on the wire
md: Wire formats fix two things: where each field sits and the byte order inside it. Pick the order in the format's specification, then convert at the edge with shifts, `from_be_bytes` or `ntohl`, and keep ordinary structs inside the program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
md: Keypoints are noisy, especially when occluded. Before writing rules on them: check per-keypoint visibility or score, prefer 3D world landmarks or a side view for sagittal angles (bends in the side-view plane that splits the body into left and right) such as the knee, smooth over a few frames, and use two thresholds (hysteresis) rather than one.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
md: Pseudonyms protect the name, not the person. They link all of one person's records, and those records (queries, routes, purchases) can identify them by content. Ask what a released record says, not only what field was deleted.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
md: Differential privacy is a property of the mechanism: on any two datasets differing in one person, every output is at most e^epsilon times likelier on one than the other. It survives post-processing and any auxiliary data, and epsilons add up across releases.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
md: Minimise by architecture: collect less, coarsen at the edge, compute on the device, separate identity from content, enforce purposes in the access layer and in database grants, and default to the least sharing.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
md: Rights are requirements on every copy: build a data map (system, lookup key, export method, erase method), meet the one-month clock (Art. 12(3)), put backups beyond use, notify recipients, and verify identity in proportion to what you would hand over.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Defending the path: segmentation, admin hygiene, EDR, HSE timeline
md: Escalation and lateral movement are a chain of small, valid-looking steps. Make each step harder (least privilege, unique and protected credentials, segmentation, patching known-exploited bugs) and make each step visible (forwarded logs, EDR, the event chains in this course), then make sure every alert has an owner.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
md: Same scores, three uses: rerank finished solutions (weighted voting is a strong default), prune partial solutions in beam search (best on harder problems at modest budgets), or provide step-level rewards so RL can credit each step separately.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Misconception: "nice 19 means it only runs when the machine is idle." A nice 19 task still has weight 15, so against one nice 0 task it gets about 1.4 percent. For truly leftover CPU, use the `SCHED_IDLE` policy, which the CFS document describes as even weaker than nice 19.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
md: Raising code size cannot fix a too-small nprobe. The paper notes that increasing the code length is useless if w is not big enough, because neighbors outside the probed lists are never scored. Tune nprobe first, then code size.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Any structural comparison in this field is after optimal superposition. A reported RMSD of 1.4 Angstrom always means 1.4 after Kabsch alignment; the unaligned number is meaningless because it depends on where the coordinates happen to be written down.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Regular expressions: counting failed logins per address
md: A per-address threshold is easy to evade. Mandiant saw UNC5537 log in mostly through commercial VPN (virtual private network) addresses, and stuffing tools can spread attempts so each address fails only once or twice. Also count failures per username, and treat any success after failures as more important than the failures themselves.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Testing your script so it does not fail silently
md: Test the awkward inputs and the failure paths, not just the happy path, and keep tests offline with fakes. A test suite is what lets you change a detection script without wondering what you broke.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Interleave, step back, or fan out: IRCoT, Step-Back and multi-query
md: Pick the pattern by the question's shape: a vague or context-dependent question needs one **rewrite**; a chain of facts needs **sequential decomposition** (Self-Ask, IRCoT); an over-specific question benefits from a **step-back**; a question that could be phrased many ways benefits from **multi-query** fan-out.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
md: A logic flaw is an assumption the server never checks. To find one, list what the design assumes about users (what they send, in what order, how fast, how many accounts) and ask which assumption would pay them to break.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Limit overrun: one coupon, one balance, many parallel requests
md: Claim-first works only because the Set lives in this one process. Run two Node processes, or two servers, or keep the state in a real database, and the check and the claim are separate network calls again. The durable fix puts the claim where the state is: a unique constraint or a conditional update in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Hidden sub-states: Kettle's GitLab email race (CVE-2022-4037)
md: Every request is a sequence of steps, so every endpoint that edits shared state has sub-states. Decide each security-relevant value once, carry it with the work, and make the state change atomic, rather than writing a value early and reading it back later.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap
md: A Raft leader commits by counting replicas **only** for entries from its own current term. Older entries become committed indirectly, when a later current-term entry after them commits. Entries keep their original term number forever, which is why this rule is needed.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
md: Per-field BM25 features are not BM25F. BM25F (the subject of Elasticsearch's `combined_fields` query) merges term frequencies across fields before saturating. Separate per-field features saturate each field on its own and let the model weigh them. Both are useful; they are different numbers.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
md: Disagreement between metrics is information, not noise. If binary metrics and exponential nDCG disagree, your system is trading coverage of relevant documents against putting the very best one first. Report at least one metric of each kind and say which user you care about.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Kaseya VSA and REvil, July 2021: one tool, many victims
md: Any tool that can run code on many machines (RMM, patch management, EDR consoles, software deployment) is Tier 0. Keep it off the internet, behind MFA and a dedicated admin network, and watch it as closely as a domain controller. CISA's MSP guidance adds: MSP accounts out of admin groups, a dedicated VPN for MSP traffic, and the MSP's activity logged into the customer's own monitoring.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
md: Polling the trailer only works if the NIC writes the message in increasing address order. FaRM notes that many NICs, including theirs, guarantee this for RDMA writes but not reads. It is a hardware property, not a verbs promise: registering memory with `IBV_ACCESS_RELAXED_ORDERING` explicitly gives up write-after-write ordering.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: Interpolation is not prediction. It never invents a position: it only blends two snapshots the server really sent. The cost is that every remote entity is shown late by the buffer delay, which is why aiming needs lag compensation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Space2 was shown only 23 times in 2000, although it is mobile users' second choice (0.25). Optimism-based exploration stops exploring once an arm looks clearly worse than the leader; that is the point, but it means some items get little data. Freshness boosts or explicit exploration slots are common additions.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Three ways to join two tables
md: Nested loop: cost about outer x inner-scan, works for any condition, great with an inner index and few outer rows. Merge join: one pass over each sorted input, needs sorted inputs and an equality key. Hash join: one pass over each input, needs an equality key and memory for the build side.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
md: $R + W > N$ is a counting argument, nothing more: if the write really sits on W of the N designated replicas and the read really asks R of those same N, they share a replica. Lesson 4 shows how failures quietly break the "same N" part.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
md: Misconception: verifiable rewards cannot be hacked. A verifier is only as strong as its isolation. If the agent can write to the tests, the test runner, the libraries they import, or read the reference answer, *pass the tests* and *solve the task* come apart.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
md: Simulate, do not multiply point estimates. The mean of the simulation is the ALE; the percentiles describe bad years; and a typical year (the median) may cost nothing at all, which is exactly why risk without numbers is easy to ignore until it happens.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
md: Read the **exceptions** and the **complementary user entity controls** (CUECs) sections of any vendor's SOC 2. Exceptions are where the auditor found a control did not operate. CUECs are controls the vendor assumes *you* perform (for example, "customers are responsible for enabling MFA for their users"); if you do not, the vendor's report does not cover that risk.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Third-party risk: questionnaires, SBOMs and concentration risk
md: A questionnaire is a vendor's own claims. "Yes" to every question from a 20-person startup is a signal to ask for evidence, not a pass. And a vendor that is excellent at security can still be a concentration risk: CrowdStrike was the security control, not the attacker. Score both "how likely is this vendor to be breached" and "what happens to us if this vendor stops working for a day".

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: A common misconception is that a bigger training cluster speeds up RL roughly linearly. Training is often a minority of the step. If generation is two-thirds of the time, even infinitely fast training saves at most a third.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Measuring achieved bandwidth with a copy kernel
md:
Common traps:
- **Arrays that fit in L2.** An 8 MB array on an H100 (50 MB L2) measures cache bandwidth, not HBM.
- **Mixing GB and GiB.** 2,982.6 GB/s is 2,777.8 GiB/s. Use one divisor for both theory and measurement.
- **Timing the first launch** or using host timers without synchronizing.
- **Uncoalesced or strided access**, which measures your access pattern, not the memory.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: RRF needs only positions. Scores on different scales, scores that drift between index versions, even systems that expose no scores at all can be fused, because $1/(k + r)$ is the same function of rank for every input.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Unsafe code is concentrated in reviewed subsystem abstractions. A driver written only against those abstractions cannot cause undefined behavior, *provided the abstractions are sound* and every `unsafe` block honours its contract. That proviso is the whole game; lesson 10 shows what happens when it fails.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: What Rust in the kernel does not prevent, and what it costs
md: Misconception: "written in Rust" means "free of memory corruption". A soundness bug in one `unsafe` block can corrupt memory exactly like C. What changes is *where to look*: the bug was in an unsafe block with a written, checkable claim, not anywhere in thousands of lines of driver logic.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: Weighted vtime in sched_ext takes a few lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Whether the weights actually hold depends on whether prev competes in `dispatch`; `scx_simple`'s does not, so on one CPU no task gets more than half.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production
md: Ignoring kernel bugs, the kernel's tools/sched_ext README puts the worst case plainly: a broken sched_ext scheduler can starve some threads until the watchdog fires. It cannot corrupt memory, and the machine returns to the fair scheduler on its own.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key hierarchies in KMS: envelope encryption and rotating the KEK
md: Two different jobs share the word rotation. Rotating a KEK limits the amount of data under one key version and lets old versions eventually be retired. Revoking access (permissions, sessions, leases) is what stops a thief. Plan both.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
md: Pickle shows up in places reviewers forget: cache layers, task queues, session stores, and machine learning model files, which are often pickles inside. "It only comes from our own cache" is true only until someone else can write to that cache.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Go: nil maps, data races and the race detector
md: Go is memory-safe only for race-free programs. In every diff, find state shared between goroutines (globals, maps in structs, caches) and confirm one lock or channel owns it. Run tests with -race, and remember it only sees the paths your tests execute.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: White-box review of a small app, end to end
md: A baseline review is the four questions applied systematically: list every entry point, check authentication and authorization on each, trace every input to every sink, then sweep the language's hazards. Tools find the dangerous calls; only the reviewer finds the missing checks.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: When the state machine forgets: Erlang/OTP SSH (CVE-2025-32433)
md: Default deny applies to protocol states as much as to firewall rules: for each state, list the messages that are allowed and reject everything else. A dispatcher that looks only at the message type is an authentication bypass waiting for someone to send messages out of order.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions and separation of duty
md: Giving a reporting job or an engineer direct write access to production tables quietly turns them into an uncertified TP. Read-only replicas for reporting, and audited break-glass access for emergencies, keep rule E1 true.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
md: Mitigation is not remediation. Volexity's disclosure warned that a mitigation "does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise". After an edge device is exploited, assume its secrets and its users' credentials are gone, and rotate them.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Testing and running automations: dry runs, caps and staged rollout
md: Put validation, never-act lists, caps, idempotency and dry run inside the action function; test the failure paths and hostile inputs; roll out in stages; and alert when an automation goes quiet.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
md: Before asking "is this secure?", ask "which asset, and which property: confidentiality, integrity or availability?" Different properties need different defences: encryption (scrambling data so only holders of a secret key can read it) mostly protects confidentiality, hashes and signatures protect integrity and authenticity, and backups and redundancy protect availability.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
md: The leak did not create the vulnerability; it created a free, reliable exploit. By the time WannaCry hit, the patch had existed for 59 days. Treat every critical advisory as if working exploit code will be public soon, because sometimes it already is.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
md: Authorisation is the line. Own it or get written, scoped permission; stop at other people's data; report privately and give owners time to fix. Practise on platforms built for it.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions
md: Do not present fear or vanity. Breach headlines from other companies and "millions of attacks blocked" both waste the board's attention. Directors respond to clear risk, honest measures and a specific ask, and they remember who was straight with them.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Why exact-match caches miss, and how a semantic cache matches meaning
md: A semantic cache trades exactness for hit rate. An exact cache never returns an answer to a different question; a semantic cache does so by design whenever two questions are close enough. The rest of this course is about where "close enough" goes wrong.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Why cloud metadata is the prize: Capital One 2019
md: "It is in a private subnet" does not protect a role's credentials. Temporary credentials from IMDS work from anywhere on the internet unless a policy restricts where they can be used. The attacker used them from their own machine.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
md: Misconception: "SGLang is a prompt DSL, so I must rewrite my app to use it." A DSL, or domain-specific language, is a small language built for one kind of job, here writing LM programs. Most of SGLang's speedups live in the runtime and apply to plain HTTP requests. The DSL is an optional layer on top.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
md: In practice the straight-line bound is weak on real road networks with travel times: it must divide by the top motorway speed, so it badly underestimates slow city streets. The Bast et al. survey reports the gain is small or nonexistent. **ALT** gets much better bounds from precomputed distances to a few landmarks plus the triangle inequality.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
md: The FFT is not an approximation. It returns the same numbers as the DFT matrix product, up to floating point rounding, by sharing work through $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
md: Misconception: "SVE code is written for a particular width like 512 bits." VLA code must never assume a length; use svcntw() and whilelt. ACLE warns that something like `svptrue_pat_b32(SV_VL16)` loads no data at all on chips narrower than 512 bits.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
md: A pool or arena that never returns memory looks like a leak from the outside. Bonwick's caches give memory back under memory pressure, when the virtual memory system runs short of free pages; your custom pool should have some way to shrink (reset, trim, or a size cap).

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
md: An alert is a question, not an answer. The analyst's job is to answer it with evidence, record the answer so someone else can check it, and feed what was learned back into the rules.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Phishing reports and unusual data egress
md: Volume alone is a weak signal; volume against the host's own baseline, plus the sending process and the destination's owner, is a strong one. Exfiltration to a popular cloud storage service will look normal by destination, so the process and the account doing the upload matter most.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
md: Warnings work when they are rare, specific and opinionated, and fail when they are frequent and neutral. Where the safe answer is always the same, block instead of warning.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
md: Misconception: "it's only dangerous if someone opens a file on the drive". Devices that present themselves as a keyboard can type commands as soon as they are connected, and a network implant needs no user action at all. Controls must act at connection time.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: Dead latents grow with width; fix them with resampling, encoder-equals-decoder-transpose init and an AuxK loss. Feature splitting means the dictionary you get depends on width, so a feature is always 'a feature at this resolution'.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: The variogram turns Tobler's law into numbers: how much readings disagree, on average, as a function of distance. Its nugget, sill and range are what kriging uses to decide weights.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
md: Speculative sampling is exact in math, not bit for bit. Chen et al. note samples match the target 'within hardware numerics': different batching, kernels and random number streams change floating point results, so a fixed seed will not reproduce plain decoding token for token.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: CTC and wav2vec 2.0: training without frame-level alignments
md: Two families: CTC models (like wav2vec 2.0 fine-tuned) classify every frame and collapse the path, so output is tied to audio frames. Encoder-decoder models (like Whisper) generate text with a decoder that also acts as a language model, which buys punctuation and multitask prompts and brings language-model failure modes such as loops.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: `free` rarely shrinks your process. Freed small chunks go back on glibc's free lists, not to the kernel, and a single live chunk near the top of the heap blocks trimming. A process whose memory never drops after a burst is usually not leaking; check whether the memory is reusable before hunting leaks.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: A non-NULL return from `malloc` does not mean the memory exists. Under default overcommit a large allocation succeeds immediately, and the failure, if any, comes later as an OOM kill when the pages are first written, far from the line that allocated them.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Misconception: "out of order is rare, so I can ignore it". In the toy, 5 of 12 readings arrive after a reading with a later event time. Mobile, battery-powered and intermittently connected devices make this the normal case, not an edge case.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: The Transformer's core bet: replace the recurrent chain with attention, so every position can read every other position in one layer and the whole layer runs as parallel matrix multiplications.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
md: A Transformer layer = attention (mix across positions) + FFN (transform each position), each wrapped in a residual connection and LayerNorm, with positional information added once at the input.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
md: Length normalization is relative to avgdl, so only a document's length compared with the average matters. An average-length document scores the same for every b.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: A GPT is just: embed (token + position), $L$ x [pre-LN causal attention, pre-LN MLP, each added to the residual stream], final LayerNorm, project back to vocabulary scores with the tied embedding matrix.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
md: A common slip is evaluating the outer derivative at $x$ instead of at the inner value. Here $f'(u) = 2u$ must use $u = 7$, giving 14, not $2 \times 2 = 4$. That is why the forward values are computed and stored first: the backward step needs them.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: A rising loss does not always mean a bug in your gradients. With a correct gradient, too large a learning rate alone makes training diverge, as $\eta = 0.35$ did here. Lowering $\eta$ is the first thing to try.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
md: Do not test your quoting in zsh and assume bash agrees. zsh, the default interactive shell on macOS, does **not** word-split unquoted parameter expansions unless the `SH_WORD_SPLIT` option is set. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/bash` or `#!/bin/sh` (a first line naming the interpreter, the shebang of lesson 4) follow the splitting rules shown here.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: `set -e` is a safety net, not error handling. It misses failures inside functions called from conditions and in `&&` chains. For steps that matter, check explicitly: `if ! cp src dst; then echo 'copy failed' >&2; exit 1; fi`.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
md: Skip-gram is not trained to be a good language model; the prediction task is a pretext. Mikolov et al. say plainly that the skip-gram model is only concerned with learning high-quality vector representations. After training, the output layer is usually thrown away and the input vectors are kept as the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: A GPU is a throughput machine. It hides slow memory by keeping many warps in flight, not by making any single access fast. Give it too little parallel work and the SMs sit idle.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
md: Bigger batches are not free for users: once the step leaves the flat region (math roof, or growing KV reads), every sequence's inter-token latency rises. A throughput number without a latency number hides this.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Decisions in machine code: flags, compare and conditional jumps
md: Misconception: "the CPU knows whether a value is signed." It does not. `cmp` sets all four flags every time; the signedness lives only in which jump the compiler chose after it.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
md: Every address your program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it on every access using the current process's page table, the TLB makes that fast, and page faults let the OS fill in memory lazily.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: The reward model learns only from differences. Its job is to rank responses to the same prompt, and its output is a log-odds score: a gap of 1 means about 73 percent preference.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
md: C is small: a handful of types, operators that work on bits and integers as directly as the CPU does, and `if`, `for`, `while`, `switch` and functions. What makes it hard is not syntax but the rules for memory, which the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: A pointer does not know how many elements it points to. Whoever passes a buffer must also pass its length (or rely on a terminator such as the zero byte), and every write must be checked against that length.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
md: `void *` carries an address without a type; the code that receives it must convert it back to the right type. A function pointer carries code. Together they let one function such as qsort work on any data, with the caller supplying the type-specific part.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership answers C's question *who frees this, and when?* statically: the single owner frees it, at the end of the owner's scope. No `free` calls, no collector.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
md: Lifetime annotations do not change how long anything lives. They describe relationships between references so the borrow checker can verify each call site. The function body is checked against the signature, and callers are checked against the signature alone.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: A vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers and also an arrow in $n$-dimensional space. Addition and scaling act component by component; the norm is the arrow's length.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
md: $\det A$ is the factor by which $A$ scales areas (negative if it flips orientation). $\det A = 0$ means a direction is squashed flat: no inverse. Otherwise $A^{-1}A = I$ and $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, but in code you call `solve`, and you watch the condition number, not the determinant.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: A loss turns "fit the data" into one number that depends on the parameters. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood for class probabilities. Training means minimizing it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Watch the **gap** between training and test (or validation: a held-out split used for tuning, see lesson 8) error. A small gap with high error means underfitting; a low training error with a large gap means overfitting. Training loss alone cannot tell you which you have.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
md: Suspiciously good validation results are a bug report until proven otherwise. Check that every preprocessing step was fit on training rows only, that no group or time period straddles the split, and that no feature is recorded after the outcome it predicts.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
md: Backprop = for each node in reverse order: upstream gradient times local gradient, summed over every path that leaves the node. One backward sweep yields the gradient for every input at once.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
md: Locks are for mutual exclusion; condition variables are for waiting until shared state changes. With a CV, always hold the lock, keep the condition in a state variable, and wait in a while loop. A semaphore can play either role, depending on its initial value.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
md: Data journaling writes every data block twice, which halves sequential write bandwidth. That is why metadata (ordered) journaling is the more common choice; OSTEP notes that Windows NTFS and SGI's XFS use forms of it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. The **covariance** $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]$, the mean product of the two deviations from their means, is positive when the two rise together and negative when one is high as the other is low. Lesson 8 develops it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
md: With little data the prior drives the answer, so state it. A prior that puts zero probability on some value can never recover it: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, and anything times 0 stays 0.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: $C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: The product of training is an **ordered list of merges**. Order matters: rank 1 is the first merge learned. The vocabulary is just the alphabet plus every merge result, and the next lesson shows that encoding new text replays this list in order.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
md: Tokenization fixes what the model can see. Vocabulary size trades sequence length against parameters; the regex and digit rules shape arithmetic; the training data mix decides which languages are cheap; and rare tokens can be under-trained.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
md: Accumulation is exactly equivalent only for layers that treat examples independently. **BatchNorm** computes statistics per micro-batch: with examples (1, 2, 3, 4) in one batch it normalizes the value 2 to -0.45, but in the micro-batch (1, 2) it becomes +1.00. The playbook also notes that accumulation gives no throughput benefit, since it runs the same small batches; it only changes the effective batch size.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
md: Links are bidirectional when added, but pruning (step 4) can later drop a link from one side. The graph is therefore directed in practice, and a node whose incoming links are all pruned becomes hard or impossible to reach. Deletions are hard for the same reason; lesson 5 shows how libraries handle them.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Reproducible builds: proving a binary came from its source
md: Reproducible builds prove the binary matches *the source you built from*. They say nothing about which source that should be. xz 5.6.1's release tarball contained a malicious build script missing from git; rebuilding the tarball reproduces the backdoor perfectly. Compare release archives against the tagged git tree too (Arch Linux switched xz to building from git when the backdoor was disclosed).

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
md: A closed loop collapses at a rate set by the sample size, and you can measure that rate. A small but steady stream of real data turns the downward drift into a stable level.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (IBRS, Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation, limits branch speculation) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: The kernel's view of your memory is a list of VMAs. `execve` and ld.so create the first ones, `mmap` adds, `munmap` removes and splits, `mprotect` splits by permission, and `mremap` resizes or moves. `/proc/PID/maps` is that list, and it is the first thing to read when a mapping misbehaves.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. A quantile is a percentile written as a fraction: the 0.99 quantile is p99. The formula is the N p at most 0.01 rule from the prediction, solved for p: each leaf may be slow at most 1/(100N) of the time. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
md: Derived numbers go stale. *Years of experience* computed at index time is wrong a month later for everyone with a current role. Store intervals with open ends and compute tenure at query time against the query's reference date, or recompute on a schedule and record the as-of date.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Thinking longer does not scale forever. s1's gains flattened after about six forced continuations, suppressing the stop too often led to repetitive loops, and the context window (the most tokens the model can read and write in one pass) caps how long one trace can be. Parallel methods (voting, PRM search over several traces) can extend scaling past that point; s1 found they complement sequential scaling.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
md: Every number here is one group's runs at 760M parameters or less. A later public reimplementation (lesson 8) found the full model did not always beat its baselines, while the memory itself consistently helped over attention-only variants.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
md: Every modern malloc fast path is the same idea as the 2001 magazine layer: a small, private stack of free objects per thread or CPU, refilled and drained in batches from a locked shared layer, with sizing policies to cap the memory that sits idle.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
md: Measure a hunt programme by what it changes: detections created, gaps and vulnerabilities closed, techniques examined, and the dwell time of anything it finds. Intrusions found matter most when they happen, but a quarter without one is not a failed quarter if the organisation is harder to attack at the end of it.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames
md: Use the kill chain to ask "where can we act against this adversary, and how many independent ways?" and ATT&CK to ask "which of their known behaviours can we see?". Both answer defender decisions, which is why they belong in intelligence products.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack surface: every door, window and vent
md: "Internal only" is not off the surface. An endpoint reachable only from inside the network is still reachable by anyone who gets inside: a phished employee, a compromised vendor login, a malicious insider. Count it, and protect it as if the network were hostile.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Third-party access is a trust boundary you do not fully control. Give each vendor the narrowest path, watch it closely, and assume the vendor's own computers may already be compromised.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A forecast is a prediction made at an origin $T$ using only data up to $T$, for a stated horizon $h$. Every evaluation in this course respects that constraint.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Reading an X.509 certificate field by field
md: Common misconception: "the CN must match the hostname". Modern clients ignore CN for name matching and check SAN only; a certificate with the right CN but no matching SAN entry fails in browsers and in Python's ssl module.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
md: `tl.load` with a mask but no `other=` leaves masked lanes **undefined**. That is safe only if those lanes never feed a result. Any reduction (sum, max) over a masked block needs `other=` set to the operation's neutral value: the value that leaves the result unchanged, 0 for a sum (x + 0 = x) and minus infinity for a max (max(x, -inf) = x).

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
md: Misconception: "lambda is just a weight, any value works." Text cross-entropy and noise MSE live on different scales, and lambda decides how the shared weights split their capacity. Transfusion used 5, BAGEL effectively 4 (0.25 CE + 1 MSE is a quarter of CE + 4 MSE). Change the noise parameterization or schedule and the right value moves.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
md: Build-time specialization = **pick components by configuration, link statically, let DCE and LTO remove the rest**. Reconfiguring means rebuilding.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
md: At hundreds of dimensions, a distance does about 0.5 to 0.75 FLOPs per byte of vector it reads. SIMD makes the arithmetic cheap; after that, the bytes you move (and the cache misses you take) decide the speed.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Turning on mmap does not shrink an index; it only lets the OS evict parts of it. If the hot working set does not fit, latency can fall off a cliff, because each miss is a disk read instead of a DRAM access.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
md: Video cost is **frames x tokens per frame**. Every long-video method attacks one factor: fewer frames (sampling), fewer tokens per frame (pooling), fewer tokens over time (merging, memory), a bigger budget (long context), or a different representation (text captions).

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
md: A ViT-B/16 backbone is 85.8M parameters, 99% of them in 12 identical blocks of 7.09M each, and two thirds of each block is MLP. The classification head is tiny: 77,669 parameters for 101 classes.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
md: Misconception: web pretraining teaches the robot new motions. It does not. Web knowledge helps decide *which* object and *where*; the motor skills themselves still come from robot demonstrations.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: FSQ and LFQ: quantizers with no learned codebook
md: FSQ and LFQ trade a learned codebook for a fixed grid. You lose the freedom to place codes where the data is dense, and gain full usage by construction, no codebook loss, and vocabularies of 2^16 to 2^18 that VQ struggles to use.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades
md: CUDA graphs constrain attention through shape (pad to a captured size), address (persistent metadata buffers) and kernel choice (`AttentionCGSupport`). The weakest backend in the model sets the graph mode for everyone.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
md: A high benchmark score does not mean the model looked at the image. The BlindTest paper cites prior work finding that 42.9% of MMMU questions can be answered without the image. Build a small eval from your own documents, with the image-free baseline as a control.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
md: Check every layer. A wait-free algorithm is only as wait-free as its primitives and helpers: a `fetch_or` that compiles to a CAS loop, an allocator that takes a lock, or a reclamation scheme that can block will each reintroduce unbounded waiting.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Web testing as work: pentests, disclosure programmes and bounties
md: A pentest buys coverage of an agreed scope; a bug bounty buys the first valid report of each root cause; a VDP buys reports without payment. In all three the written rules, published or signed before testing, are what make the work legal.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: File inclusion: when a path parameter chooses the code that runs
md: Path traversal reads a file; file inclusion runs it. The fix for both is the same idea: the user picks from a list the server owns, never a path.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Origins and sites: how the browser names who owns a page
md: Same-site is not same-origin. `login.example.com` and `blog.example.com` are same-site but cross-origin. A weak subdomain (an old blog, a marketing page run by a vendor) is "same-site" with your login page, and cookie rules and SameSite (lesson 5) treat it as a friend.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Site isolation: separate processes as a second wall
md: Site isolation is **defence in depth** for the browser itself. It does not change what web pages are allowed to do, so it will not stop XSS, CSRF or a bad CORS policy. It limits the damage when the browser's own enforcement fails.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: SMB file shares and EternalBlue: how WannaCry spread
md: Worms need two things: a reachable service and a bug in it. Patching removes the bug; turning off SMBv1 and blocking 445 removes the reachability. Do both, because you will never patch everything on time.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Public Wi-Fi and captive portals in the HTTPS era
md: On public Wi-Fi, TLS with correct certificate validation is what protects you, not the Wi-Fi layer. The risks that remain are the places where TLS is missing (first HTTP request, portal page) or broken (apps that skip validation).

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Misconception: more workers always means more throughput. With one locked queue, past the knee extra workers only add waiters on the same lock and the same cache line. The model here is deliberately simple, but the cap of 1/c is real for any serial section.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
md: WSD is **not fully schedule-free**. Optimal peak LR still shifts with training length: Bergsma et al. (2025) quote Shen et al. puzzling that the best WSD LRs differ by token count, and Hägele et al. found the best cooldown peak LR was about half the best cosine peak. Tune the peak LR at roughly the length you care about; lesson 7 gives the evidence and a rule for adjusting it.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
md: Writing into a buffer before its id completes does not crash anything, but it corrupts your own stream: the modified bytes may go out on the wire or in a retransmission. The kernel docs: kernel integrity is not affected, but a buggy program can corrupt its own data stream.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
md: Zero-shot replaces training data with design choices. Make those choices on a labeled dev set: compare templates or descriptions, pick argmax or per-label thresholds by the cost of errors, and re-check whenever the labels change.
